messages.content:
Forecast date: 2026-02-05. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.

content.thinking:
Let me think about this carefully. The question asks about AI contributing a substantive new mathematical argument to a correct, complete solution of one of the remaining Millennium Prize Problems.

These are extremely hard problems. Let me consider each timeline:

2026: Less than a year away. Extremely unlikely any of these gets solved with AI contribution in this timeframe.

2030: AI capabilities will be significantly greater. But these problems are incredibly deep. Even with AI assistance, solving any of these by 2030 seems quite unlikely but not impossible.

2035: More time for AI to develop. Possible but still challenging.

2040: AI systems could be very capable by then.

2050: Long timeline, significant AI advancement likely.
These problems likely need fundamentally new mathematical ideas rather than pattern-matching or computational search, and the bar here is AI genuinely contributing to a solution, not just brute-forcing it. Given how little progress even top human mathematicians have made on most of these despite decades of effort, I'd put rough probabilities around 0.5% by 2026, 4% by 2030, 10% by 2035, and 20% by 2040.

By 2050, with several more decades of AI capability growth, I'd estimate around 35% -- substantial progress becomes plausible, though these problems could easily remain open that long.
